summary: Defines Negative Trust Anchors, which let an operator turn off DNSSEC validation for specific domains. They are used to work around validation failures caused by a domain's own signing mistakes, so users can still reach it.

plainLanguage.summary: If a friend's doorbell is broken, you knock on the door instead of giving up. This lets you skip the broken check for one site.

subtitle: A temporary, local switch that lets a resolver skip DNSSEC validation for one broken domain without turning validation off everywhere.

tldr.problem: When a domain makes a DNSSEC signing mistake, validating resolvers refuse to answer for it, and users blame their ISP and may switch to a resolver that does no validation at all.
tldr.mechanism: A Negative Trust Anchor (NTA) is configured locally on a validating resolver. The resolver treats the named domain and everything below it as unsigned and does not set the AD bit, while validation stays on for all other names.
tldr.outcome: Access is restored quickly while the domain owner fixes the error. NTAs are meant to be short-lived, must expire automatically and should not last more than a week.

today: RFC 7646 is an Informational RFC and no later RFC is recorded as obsoleting or updating it, so it remains the reference definition of Negative Trust Anchors.

sections.title: Why Validation Failures Hurt
sections.content:
DNSSEC signing tools and processes are less mature than the rest of DNS administration. When a domain mismanages its DNSSEC records, a validating resolver correctly refuses to answer, and many users cannot reach the domain.

Users usually blame their ISP or resolver operator. They may complain, or switch to a non-validating resolver. The RFC says this is bad advice: a domain can also fail validation because of an attack, so switching resolvers can harm security. Without a tool like the NTA, this pressure may lead an operator to disable DNSSEC validation or never deploy it.
sections.plainLanguage: A lock checker at the gate sometimes stops people because the site's own paperwork is wrong. People get cross with the gate keeper, and some tell everyone to remove the checker. That would let real bad guys in too.

sections.title: What a Negative Trust Anchor Is
sections.content:
A normal trust anchor is the starting point a validating resolver uses to build the chain of authentication for a signed answer. An NTA does the opposite: it stops validation at a chosen name. The resolver treats upstream responses as if the zone were unsigned and does not set the Authentic Data (AD) bit in the answers it sends to clients.

An NTA is a behavior, not a new resource record. It can sit at any level of the chain of trust and applies from that point down. A positive trust anchor further down switches validation back on: with an NTA at example.com and a positive trust anchor at foo.bar.example.com, validation resumes for foo.bar.example.com and below.

NTAs are configured locally by the organization that needs one and are not distributed outside its administrative boundary. They concern DNSSEC only, not X.509 PKI.
sections.plainLanguage: An NTA is a note on the checker's desk that says: for this one street, stop checking IDs for now. The note stays inside your own building and is not passed around.

sections.title: When and How to Use One
sections.content:
Trained DNS staff must first confirm that the failure is a misconfiguration and not an attacker who has taken over the domain's servers. They should also confirm the domain is not intentionally broken for testing, and should make a reasonable attempt to contact the domain owner, preferably before putting the NTA in place. The RFC notes that this is a rare event, usually about once per quarter or less.

For a broken TLD or a very popular domain, it may be appropriate to use an NTA as soon as the misconfiguration is confirmed.

The rules in Section 2.1 are firm:

  • An NTA MUST only be used for a limited duration, and implementors SHOULD let the operator set an end time and date.
  • Use of an NTA MUST NOT be automatic.
  • An NTA SHOULD cover only a specific domain or subdomain and MUST NOT affect validation of names up the chain. An NTA for zone1.example.com still leaves validation on for example.com, .com and the root.

An NTA placed where a positive trust anchor is configured MUST take precedence over it. Implementations may warn about this. Operators should also consider publicly disclosing current and past NTAs, since there is no special DNS response code that tells a client an NTA is in place.
sections.plainLanguage: Before skipping the check, a grown-up must make sure it is only a paperwork mistake and not a trick, and should try to tell the site owner. The skip is for one street only and always has an end date. It never switches on by itself.

sections.title: Removing an NTA
sections.content:
An NTA must not linger. NTAs MUST expire automatically when their configured lifetime ends, and the lifetime SHOULD NOT exceed a week. The RFC says experience is limited and that at least one large vendor documented customer feedback suggesting a week is reasonable.

It is RECOMMENDED that implementations periodically try to validate the domain while the NTA is in place. One suggested method is a periodic query for the SOA record at the NTA node. If the resolver gets an answer it can validate (including a NOERROR/NODATA answer with proper NSEC or NSEC3 records), it presumes the NTA is no longer needed and removes it. Implementations SHOULD do this by default, but should let operators override it, because a name like www.example.com can have a bad signature while the SOA at example.com is fine.

When removing an NTA, the implementation SHOULD remove all cached entries at and below the NTA node.
sections.plainLanguage: The skip note has an expiry date, and the checker keeps peeking to see whether the street fixed its paperwork. As soon as it has, the note is thrown away.

sections.title: Telling a Mistake from an Attack
sections.content:
The RFC stresses that discovering whether a failure is an operator error or an attack is not trivial and that no simple checklist exists. Clues it lists include whether the failure is the same across different software, whether it shows consistently from around the world and from all authoritative servers, and whether the actual answer data changed. A consistent error is more likely an operator mistake; authoritative output that differs from what resolvers see hints at an attack, unless EDNS0 client subnet is in use.

Common operator errors it names are expired RRSIG signatures, and DNSKEY records in a child zone that do not match the DS record in the parent, often during key rollovers. Tools it mentions include DNSViz, the Verisign DNSSEC debugger and Zonemaster.

Intentionally broken test domains such as dnssec-failed.org should fail with SERVFAIL (RCODE 2) on a validating resolver. Operators should not add NTAs for them.
sections.plainLanguage: The grown-up acts like a detective. If the same mistake shows up everywhere and the site did not change, it is probably just a slip. If different people see different things, someone may be tricking them.

sections.title: Security Trade-offs
sections.content:
While an NTA is active, DNSSEC validation is effectively off for that domain. There can also be a gap between the day the domain is fixed and the day the NTA is removed. An NTA can be put in place without the domain administrator knowing, which is why the RFC says attempts SHOULD be made to contact and inform them first.

A side effect is that applications that expect the AD bit for a domain may break. The RFC expects that many applications that require DNSSEC perform their own validation, so this should not be a major problem.
sections.plainLanguage: While the note is up, that street is not being checked, so it should be short and the site owner should know about it. Apps that need to be extra sure usually do their own checking anyway.
